sources.title: Faster to Science: A Letter to the Science Community

discussion.body: The tension worth watching is speed against rigor. The same plan keeps cost and schedule control mandatory across every mission class, with breaches carrying consequences up to and including mission termination. Faster selection does not mean a softer leash.

Equal footing for first-time teams is the selling line, but implementing organizations are also evaluated on past performance on projects of similar complexity and cost. That is a thumb on the scale for the usual suspects, however clean the science-only pitch sounds.

items.title: NASA's Competition Model 2.0: Judge the Science First, Write the Engineering Plan Later
items.body:
NASA says it wants to deliver science faster, so it is changing how it competes for and selects missions, starting from a simple premise: compete on the science first.

Proposals under the new model are science-focused, and detailed engineering, cost and implementation work is not required until it is genuinely needed to make a decision.

One set of missions moves to a new, accelerated two-step competition, an update NASA expects to cut the time to step-2 selection by as much as 45 percent. The biggest missions are carved out: CM2.0 does not change how they are managed, because NASA says that process was already reformed.

sources.title: The real reasons US politicians are getting older

discussion.body: The striking statistic is not any single member's age but the pipeline behind them. Among comparable democracies, the US has one of the lowest proportions of lawmakers under 45, which is what a gerontocracy looks like when you measure it instead of arguing about it.

Concern about the age and health of some politicians has run through both Republican and Democratic circles and revived talk of age limits or health checks. But if the electorate itself skews older, it is not obviously the constituency that will demand them.

items.title: The Average US Representative Is 58, the Average Senator 65, and the Trend Runs Upward
items.body:
Congressional records show the lowest median ages in both chambers were recorded in the early 1980s, at 48 in the House and 52 in the Senate.

The median age of Congress members has ticked upward over time since then, and Pew Research Center analysis puts the average age at the start of the current Congress at 58 for a House member and 65 for a senator.

Set beside those figures, one demographic parallel stands out: the profile of people who actually vote tends to skew older, much like the elected officials themselves.

sources.title: The Justice Department begins notifying counties where it wants to monitor elections

discussion.body: The procedural question could decide more than the political one: Colorado officials say they are weighing how to respond, since state rules require observers to have permission from the secretary of state unless a court orders them in. The department says it will share the specifics closer to the election, which leaves states very little room to argue about the rules.

Adams County, Colo., is on the list, and its clerk — Democrat Josh Zygielbaum — said he was not surprised, because the county sits inside the 8th Congressional District, a toss-up that could decide which party controls the House next year. Permission slips and district maps: the second one is what everyone will really be watching.

items.title: The DOJ Planned 1,000 Observers Nationwide; Notifications Have Started
items.body:
The Justice Department this week began telling counties that it wants to monitor their elections on Election Day, NPR reports. Last month Harmeet Dhillon, who leads the department's Civil Rights Division, said it planned to send 1,000 observers nationwide — the largest monitoring effort in DOJ history, as she described it.

Counties in Colorado, Florida, Minnesota, Texas and Washington have received notifications so far, and the list appears to be growing in real time. Which jurisdictions, and how many, the department will actually monitor in November remains unclear.

sources.title: Tesla profits drop 43% in Q3

discussion.body: The mix is the more interesting number: automotive revenue slipped 3 percent to $20.6 billion, while services and other — parts, Supercharger use — grew by a third to $4.6 billion. There is a services business quietly outgrowing the car business inside the same income statement.
Tesla sold fewer cars than a year earlier and still beat analyst projections, so demand is not the wound here. A 110 percent jump in capital spending reads more like a deliberate bet than a squeeze.

Solar panels and storage had been a growth line, and their revenue fell 16 percent year over year to $2.9 billion. That is the number that complicates a pure spending story — a business that was expanding, going backwards, deserves an explanation.

items.title: Tesla's Profit Fell 43% While Revenue Barely Moved
items.body:
Tesla's third-quarter 2026 results put revenue at $28 billion, almost unchanged from the same quarter of 2025. Net profit fell to $787 million, down 43 percent year over year.

Operating expenses rose 39 percent to $4.8 billion, cutting Tesla's operating margin to 2.6 percent, down from 5.8 percent a year earlier.

Capital expenditures climbed 110 percent to $4.7 billion, and free cash flow dropped 62 percent to $1.5 billion. That is a company spending hard on its future while the profit line thins.

sources.title: US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate

discussion.body:
Notice how narrow the order is: non-emergency government employees and their families, not a full pullout.

The State Department's warning that the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly is the sentence that ages worst if they do.

There is a stated reason on the Houthi side: the group said it was retaliating for what it calls a Saudi blockade of its territory and for an airstrike on Sanaa airport that it blamed on the kingdom.

The conflict itself is old — it began when the Houthis ousted Yemen's government from the capital, Sanaa, in 2014.

items.title: US Orders Non-Emergency Staff and Families Out of Saudi Arabia Amid Rising Houthi Conflict
items.body:
The US State Department has issued an ordered departure for non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia, a spokesperson said in a statement.

Saudi authorities said debris from a drone intercepted during an attempted attack on an oil field killed two people, while one person died after a strike at the King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.

Conflict between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia has been rising over the past month, with the Houthis answering Saudi strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases inside the kingdom.

sources.title: A company says its polls were fake. Here's what happened

discussion.body: Wedgewood framed it as a hypothesis: how easy is it for an entirely fabricated polling firm to gain traction, be taken seriously, and expose how little scrutiny exists in media and public commentary? Its own answer, posted to X, was that it was far too easy — which reads less like a confession than like a charge sheet against everyone else.

FiftyPlusOne contests the premise that nobody looked. It refuted Wedgewood's claim that its site and The New York Times had absorbed the polling data without verifying the source, the methodology, or whether the firm was legitimate.

Intent aside, the numbers had real recipients. Mallory McMorrow, a Democratic state senator in Michigan, wrote that a Wedgewood poll in June showed her plummeting into single digits, which she said conflicted with her campaign's internals; she suspended her Senate campaign in July, about a month before the primary that Abdul El-Sayed won.

items.title: Wedgewood Polling Says the Vast Majority of Its Data Was Fabricated, Calling It an Experiment
items.body:
Wedgewood Polling, whose polls had been cited by national news outlets, said the vast majority of its data had been fabricated, describing the operation as an experimental project meant to demonstrate the vulnerabilities of the modern political polling industry. It released that statement after FiftyPlusOne, a polling and election analysis site, questioned the veracity of the firm's results.

Andrew Gelman, a professor of statistics and political science at Columbia University, questioned Wedgewood's account that the whole thing had always been intended as an experiment.

sources.title: Nurse describes crowded, chaotic hospital ER at fatality inquiry for Edmonton man

discussion.body: That schedule assumes a quiet department. Reassessing patients within recommended time frames can be impractical exactly when waiting rooms are crowded, so the fuller the room gets, the further behind the clock falls.

Tightening the triage timetable may not be the fix. Shang said ERs cannot simply close their doors when they reach capacity, and called the department the canary in the coal mine — the place where problems from the broader health-care system ultimately surface.

items.title: About Eight Hours in a Crowded Edmonton ER, and a Reassessment Schedule Built for 10 to 12 Patients an Hour
items.body:
Prashant Sreekumar, 44, died at Grey Nuns Community Hospital on Dec. 22, 2025, after collapsing in the ER while experiencing chest pain. He had waited about eight hours to be seen by a doctor, and a triage nurse described conditions in the Edmonton emergency room that day as noisy, unruly and crowded.

His death is being examined by Justice Randal Brandt at a fatality inquiry at the Edmonton Court of Justice.

Beil said a two- to three-minute reassessment every 30 minutes is supposed to let a nurse see about 10 to 12 patients an hour, leaving little possibility of meeting those timelines when more patients are waiting.

sources.title: FCC chair warns media not to run the "fake polls" Trump keeps complaining about

discussion.body: The wording is doing two jobs at once: 'advised' is soft, but 'News Distortions' and 'Broadcast Hoaxes' are not, and a post that tells journalists their polls lack 'a scientific, accurate, or even real basis' is not really a suggestion. Anyone on the receiving end has to decide how much of a warning this is, and the phrase 'regulatory obligations' is the part that will keep a news director up at night.

The simplest reading is less conspiratorial: Carr asked broadcasters to give viewers more context about polls they had covered. And the hoax was real — a small polling outfit was exposed this week, after a similar case in August — and news outlets did report on those hoaxes, which is exactly the context being demanded.

items.title: The FCC Chair Warns Broadcasters About Airing 'Fake Polls'
items.body:
The chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, Brendan Carr, warned broadcasters about airing 'fake polls,' amplifying one of the complaints President Trump has regularly made about the news media. In a post on X, Carr said that many journalists and broadcasters have been airing those polls 'without regard to basic journalistic ethics' and without informing the public that the polls lack a scientific, accurate or even real basis. Broadcasters, he advised, should avoid 'News Distortions' or 'Broadcast Hoaxes' by airing polls that would violate their regulatory obligations.

One small polling outfit was exposed as a hoax this week, and a similar incident occurred in August. The standard Carr points to is not a new one — it is whatever a broadcaster's existing regulatory obligations already require; the striking part is who is offering the reminder, and in what vocabulary.

A sitting FCC chairman telling broadcasters which polls are legitimate is a notable escalation of a president's running complaint into a regulator's mouth. The reminder also lands on real ground: polling that was invented and then exposed is a genuine problem for any newsroom that aired it.

sources.title: ‘I’d consider replacing one of my children’: Taika Waititi on robot kids, his cheese-o-meter and Klara and the Sun

discussion.body: Loyalty to the book is a critic's ledger, and the festival crowd keeps a different one: at the London film festival, a group of young influencers trading highlights agreed on Klara and the Sun, calling it funny and moving, their favourite so far.
They had also gathered to meet the film's creators and stars, and affection on that footing is not a verdict. The paper's own critic, who loved the novel, left less convinced by the screen version.

items.title: Ishiguro on Why Adaptations Fail: 'Sometimes It's Not Just Loyalty but Laziness'
items.body:
Ishiguro has watched several of his books become films, among them The Remains of the Day, Never Let Me Go and A Pale View of Hills. His account of the results is unsentimental: the best films break away from the book and the worst are too faithful, a failure he describes as 'not just loyalty but laziness.'

A transcription is not an interpretation. You can't simply have the text in front of you, he says; you need imagination to move it on. A film, in his telling, has to step out of the book 'on a journey to being something bigger.'

Whether that journey paid off is precisely what is contested: the Guardian's critic loved Ishiguro's 'distinctively spare and poignant' source novel and found Waititi's screen version less convincing — 'certainly noisy.'

sources.title: Corporate ‘orbital data centre’ proposals are dangerous for humanity

discussion.body: The strangest artefact here is a licensing document that repeats the applicant’s cosmic vocabulary back at it. Paperwork doing the marketing is a genre of its own.

Betting is the operative word: these are proposals and ambitions, not achievements. And the technology is untested, with some proposed satellites twice the size of the International Space Station, which is a lot of hardware to promise on the strength of a nice idea.

items.title: SpaceX's Million-Satellite Filing Borrows a Scale Built for Alien Civilizations
items.body:
More American companies are betting they can beat the laws of physics by launching thousands of enormous satellites to create orbital “AI data centres,” according to The Conversation Canada, with names like Cowboy Space’s Stampede. SpaceX’s own filing asks for one million satellites and invokes the hypothetical Kardashev scale — a measure originally proposed to gauge an alien civilization’s level of technological advancement — in language the outlet likens to teenage fan fiction rather than a serious government document.

According to the article, the United States Federal Communications Commission repeated that language back when it filed acceptance documents, stating that the satellite system would represent a “first step towards becoming a Kardashev II-level civilization – one that can harness the Sun’s full power.”

sources.title: Stevie Van Zandt: ‘My religion switched right over to rock’n’roll’

discussion.body: The category change is what stays with me: the same injustice could have been one more subject for the next album, and he says it stopped being an intellectual exercise instead. That is a higher bar than a good protest song, and it is why “I became an activist” lands harder than any lyric would.

The absolutism is the part I would argue with. “No reform is going to fix this” is the most flattering sentence available to an activist, because it turns a verdict into a substitute for the dull work. All the same, for a man the Guardian presents as a consigliere twice over, taking the hardest line for once is a real departure.

items.title: Stevie Van Zandt's Activist Turn Began With a Cab Ride in South Africa
items.body:
The Guardian introduces Stevie Van Zandt as a man unique in one respect — consigliere to both Bruce Springsteen and Tony Soprano — and reports that his political awakening came four decades ago in white-minority-rule South Africa.

The scene he recalls from that trip is a cab ride in which a Black man stepped off the kerb and the driver swerved to try to hit him. “At that point I became an activist,” he says, adding that there was no fixing it and no reform that was going to fix it.

sources.title: Poll: Voters want Congress to be a check on Trump, trust Democrats more on issues

discussion.body: That mood shows up in the head-to-head numbers too: less than two weeks out from Election Day, voters preferred a Democratic Congress over a Republican one 52 per cent to 41 per cent among registered voters, and 54 to 42 among likely voters. Trump's own approval sits at 34 per cent, with 62 per cent disapproving — half of all respondents strongly.

Some of this looks like buyer's remorse: nearly one in 10 people who said they voted in the 2024 presidential race regret their choice, including almost 15 per cent of self-described Trump voters. But 20 per cent say neither party cares about people like them, which is a reminder that wanting a check on Trump is not the same as enthusiasm for the alternative.

items.title: More Voters Want the Next Congress to Check Trump Than to Help Him
items.body:
The latest Strength In Numbers/Verasight poll, shared with NPR, finds record-low trust in Republicans' ability to handle voters' top issues such as immigration and rising prices. The survey of 2,028 respondents was conducted Oct. 13-19 and has a margin of sampling error of 2.2 percentage points.

Asked what they want from the next Congress, 58 per cent said it was more important to elect one that would act as a check and balance on Trump, against 25 per cent who preferred a Congress that would help him pass his agenda.

sources.title: Securing Quick access from corporate networks with AWS PrivateLink

discussion.body: The selling point is risk reduction rather than novelty: for many enterprises, routing traffic over the public internet introduces unacceptable risk. The private path still comes with an asterisk — not every Quick API is available through the API VPC endpoint, so anything built on top of the unsupported calls keeps a foot outside the wall.

That asterisk is not the only design constraint. VPC endpoints have to sit in the same AWS Region where the Quick account is deployed. Security groups also have to restrict traffic on the endpoint network interfaces to only the required ports and source ranges.

items.title: Four Building Blocks for Keeping Amazon Quick Off the Public Internet
items.body: The problem starts with a bind AWS describes plainly: enterprise data behind a corporate firewall or in a private on-premises data center has no direct network path to AWS, even though the AI agents and dashboards in Amazon Quick can query virtually any data source. The walkthrough assembles a private path from four building blocks, in order: VPC endpoints for user and API access, VPC connections for data source access, VPC endpoints for AWS data services, and outbound access to required external domains. Endpoints powered by PrivateLink carry the user-facing side — the website, API calls and embedded content — so people reaching the Quick console don't have to traverse the public internet at all.

sources.title: In her riding, United Conservative Party leaders back Danielle Smith

discussion.body: Smith publicly backed the remain option during the referendum, and the opposition NDP still criticizes her for letting the question move ahead in the first place — which makes the closing-the-file moment look more like cleanup than conversion. And the file may not stay closed: some prominent separatists have floated greater participation inside the UCP as the next step after their projected loss this week.

Separatists aren't the only count that matters. The UCP riding association for Highwood passed a motion last month calling for a leadership review, and at least 22 associations must support it for the motion to come forward at the party's AGM in late November.

items.title: About 75% Remain, and Premier Danielle Smith Tells Separatists in Her Party to Stand Down
items.body:
In Monday's referendum, about 75 per cent of voters across the province cast ballots in favour of Alberta remaining a province of Canada, according to preliminary results — a three-to-one decision against holding a formal separation vote. The numbers are preliminary.

Premier Danielle Smith is calling on separatists within her own party to stand down. Members can form their own opinions, she said, but those who keep publicly calling for separation won't be welcome as candidates or as members of local boards ahead of the 2027 election.

sources.title: 5 production challenges in multi-agent systems and how Deep Insight solved them

discussion.body: Passing only compressed results onward is the design decision I'd watch closest. Compression is an editorial act, and whatever an agent decides to squeeze out of its summary never reaches the next one.
The roster is the counterweight: there is a Coder and a Validator, and validating calculations is a listed step, so verification gets its own seat instead of being left to whoever wrote the analysis.

items.title: An Agent in Days, a Wall in Production, and Deep Insight's Eight Agents
items.body:
Open source frameworks and cloud services mean you can set up an agent in a matter of days. Moving beyond a pilot into real business applications is where teams hit a familiar wall.

Deep Insight is one proposed answer: eight agents collaborating to produce a single deliverable. Each agent works in its own independent context, does only its specialized tasks, and passes only compressed results onward.

The roster runs from a Coordinator and Planner through a Supervisor, Coder, Validator, Reporter and Tracker. Together they load the data, run analyses, generate charts, validate calculations and produce a report with citations.

sources.title: Hur Jin-ho Thanks Singapore Festival for Protecting Freedom of Expression as ‘The Assassin(s)’ Opens, SGIFF Chair Boo Junfeng Says: ‘We Refuse to Show Anything That Has Been Censored’

discussion.body: Festival chair Boo Junfeng told the opening-night audience that the team had been flooded with messages from a group in South Korea pressing it to cancel the screening, and had also received many notes of support. He thanked Hur and his team for making the trip despite the pressures back at home. The pressure was not unanimous, which is what makes the festival's decision look less like stubbornness and more like judgment.

Keep straight what the festival actually argued: it said it had carefully considered the various arguments, sees the film as an artistic interpretation of historical events, and respects the makers' creative vision. That is a defense of a particular kind of filmmaking as much as of free expression — the claim is not only that the festival may show the film, but that the film is interpreting rather than testifying.

items.title: A South Korean political thriller opened the Singapore International Film Festival two weeks after Korea's conservative opposition asked it to be pul—
items.body:
The opposition People Power Party's Oct. 6 letter went to festival executive director Jeremy Chua on behalf of all 109 of its lawmakers, asking SGIFF to reverse the selection.

The festival kept the film. In an Oct. 7 statement it said the selection had come through SGIFF's independent curatorial process, for its artistic merit and its contribution to contemporary Asian cinema.

sources.title: Vietnamese Whodunit ‘Karaoke Murder’ Sets Record With Same-Weekend Opening on Four Continents (EXCLUSIVE)

discussion.body: Karaoke is a sharper engine for a mystery than it first looks. The producers say they built the story around the pastime because of the place it holds in Vietnamese life: singing sessions are part of weddings, birthdays and Lunar New Year, as well as ordinary Sunday afternoons, and nearly every household owns a speaker and microphone. Put a killing inside a room almost everyone already has at home and the audience walks in half-way invested.

That cozy reading carries a lot of weight. The same pastime causes friction, per the producers: Vietnam penalizes noise after 10 p.m., karaoke ranks among the most common causes of rows between neighbours, and news outlets report karaoke disputes ending in tragedy every year. Borrowing the shared habit for suspense also means borrowing a real neighbourhood grievance.

items.title: Vietnam's “Karaoke Murder” opens on four continents the same weekend, a first its backers are claiming
items.body:
The Vietnamese whodunit “Karaoke Murder” will open in cinemas across North America, Europe, Australia and Asia on the same weekend, which its backers call a first for a film from Vietnam. At home, where it is titled “Án Mạng Karaoke,” it bows nationwide on Oct. 30.

The film is set on a mountain pilgrimage taken by a group of neighbours, and follows a former journalist who has to put her old investigative skills back to work after a widely loathed, karaoke-obsessed tycoon is killed overnight. Cut off from the outside world, the group turns its suspicion on everyone.

sources.title: NASA to Conduct NCAA Flyover, Engage Fans at University of Alabama

discussion.body: Three fighter jets and the boss at the stick is a recruiting poster, not an engineering update, but the aeronautics framing is at least honest about which part of the agency is doing the flying.

The low-effort way in is the NASA Experience Zone, supported by Marshall Space Flight Center: it runs 10:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. CDT and needs no game ticket, which is a cheaper introduction to the agency than a stadium flyover.

items.title: NASA's Administrator Will Pilot an F-5 in a College Football Flyover
items.body:
The flyover is part of the agency's Inspiration Tour and is set for the University of Alabama vs. Texas A&M football game in Tuscaloosa on Saturday, Oct. 24. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman will fly one of three F-5 fighter jets, a display the agency frames as highlighting its contributions to aeronautics and its commitment to advancing aviation technologies.

The tour is scheduled to culminate in MAX POWER, described as a public exposition of American air and space innovation, on Nov. 7 and 8 on and near NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

sources.title: Two Assholes Lost in the Woods: An Oral History of ‘Pine Barrens’

discussion.body: Chase's fairy tale framing comes with a catch, since unlike a fairy tale this one carries no moral — and that missing moral is exactly why the hour lodges in your head.

The no-moral reading is tidy but a bit grand. The actual engine is two men in the woods who spend the whole night threatening each other and then walk out together at first light, which is a joke about how little the crisis changed either of them.

items.title: 'Pine Barrens': An Anti-Buddy Comedy That's Also a Living Nightmare
items.body:
Two mobsters chase a seemingly invincible man through the South Jersey forest, and he vanishes, leaving only a trail of blood. As day turns into night and cold into much colder, they abandon the search for survival mode, bonding, bickering and threatening each other until they are finally rescued in the light of the next morning.

David Chase, the show's creator, reaches for a different register entirely: in the woods, in the snow, he says, it has a fairy tale quality.

sources.title: Why it pays to read for acrostics in the Classics

discussion.body: The unease was not abstract. The essay notes that St Jerome felt compelled to abandon the classical authors he loved after a nightmare vision in which the judge accused him of being a Ciceronian, not a Christian.

But Jerome's fear had an escape hatch. The essay points out that Vergil's Fourth Eclogue, portraying the birth of a miraculous boy sent from heaven to inaugurate a new Golden Age, was read from late antiquity until the 18th century as a pagan prophecy of the birth of Christ, which allowed Christianity to assimilate the Classics rather than merely reject them.

items.title: The Isaiah Acrostic a Student Found in Vergil's Georgics
items.body:
In an Aeon essay, the author recalls Richard Thomas, who had just given a talk at Baylor University, mentioning that a student of his had discovered an 'Isaiah acrostic' in Vergil's Georgics, a first-century BCE poem ostensibly about farming but really about life and the universe. That remark, the author writes, opened the door to two phenomena in ancient Greek and Latin poetry the author had not really thought about despite a lifelong career in Classics: acrostics and Judaism.

The relationship between the biblical and the classical traditions has always been fraught, the essay notes. Tertullian put the tension bluntly in his attack on pagan writers, asking what Athens has to do with Jerusalem.
